source_title: Jawbone's demise a case of 'death by overfunding' in Silicon Valley
publisher_issuer: CNBC (reporting corroborating The Information and Reuters)
company_context: Jawbone was a consumer-hardware startup known for Bluetooth speakers, headsets, and the UP fitness wearables. After raising more than $900 million and reaching a roughly $3 billion valuation by early 2015, it entered liquidation in July 2017, undone by manufacturing problems and competition from Fitbit and Apple Watch.
evidence_summary: Despite raising over $900 million and a peak valuation around $3 billion with ~450 employees in early 2015, Jawbone could not ship reliably and was outcompeted in wearables by Fitbit and the Apple Watch. Demand for its core products collapsed against better-executed rivals while its cost structure and manufacturing problems persisted, leading to liquidation in July 2017. Reporting frames it as 'death by overfunding' - capital sustained a structurally uncompetitive hardware business past the point of viability.
outcome_evidence: Jawbone began liquidation in July 2017 after failing to secure further funding; first reported by The Information and independently confirmed by Reuters. It had raised over $900 million and reached ~$3 billion valuation with ~450 employees in early 2015 before its decline.
source_limitations: The CNBC primary article returned 403 to direct WebFetch here; figures were confirmed verbatim via credible WebSearch snippets (CNBC, Fortune, TechCrunch) which themselves cite The Information and Reuters. Funding is stated as 'more than $900 million.' The diagnosis bucket (unit_economics_failure) reflects the competitive/cost-structure framing; the outcome_category (14, market/demand shift) reflects the competitive demand collapse to Fitbit/Apple.
directly_stated: ~$3 billion valuation and ~450 employees by early 2015
Manufacturing issues and competition from Apple Watch and Fitbit cited as causes
First reported by The Information, confirmed by Reuters
inferred: Excess capital prolonged an uncompetitive hardware cost structure ('death by overfunding')
Loss of product differentiation drove a demand collapse the balance sheet could not offset
why_useful_for_opsiq: Consumer-hardware case blending competitive demand collapse with weak unit economics, where heavy funding masked deterioration. Tests whether a system recognizes that abundant capital can hide rather than fix a structural competitiveness/margin problem, and links a market/demand shift to the underlying cost structure.
